title: Whale Safe rates daily whale presence in the Santa Barbara Channel from automated call detection, sightings and a habitat model to support voluntary ship slow-downs; cooperation figures for the wider program range from 59% to 85%
summary: Whale Safe, launched on 17 September 2020, uses automated whale-call detection and other data to rate whale presence daily and to grade ships' cooperation with voluntary 10-knot zones.
account: The Benioff Ocean Initiative (now the Benioff Ocean Science Laboratory) at UC Santa Barbara built Whale Safe. Its partners were Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, UC Santa Cruz, the University of Washington, the Southwest Fisheries Science Center of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and Conserve.io. Whale Safe supports NOAA's voluntary 10-knot speed reduction zone in the Santa Barbara Channel. That voluntary program predates Whale Safe (2007 onward, according to UC Santa Barbara). Whale Safe was launched on 17 September 2020 (Mongabay, 23 September 2020). Cascadia's John Calambokidis told Mongabay in 2020 that voluntary slow-downs “haven't been very effective”. Whale Safe's methodology page describes a moored acoustic buoy whose “tiny computer” detects and classifies blue, humpback and fin whale calls. Next, “An analyst then reviews these data and indicates for each 15-minute period whether each of the monitored species was detected”. The page also describes naturalist sightings through the Whale Alert and Spotter Pro apps, NOAA aerial surveys and the WhaleWatch 2.0 blue whale habitat model. These feed a daily Whale Presence Rating. Ship-tracking data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS) are used to grade each vessel's “cooperation rate” with the voluntary zone. UC Santa Barbara's news office (21 September 2022) called the buoy system “AI-powered”. It quoted director Douglas McCauley: “Every year since the original launch of Whale Safe we have seen an increase in ship cooperation rates”. KCBX (11 April 2024) reported from Whale Safe data: “in 2023, large vessels only slowed down 59% of the time in designated slow speed zones”. The Santa Barbara Independent (16 July 2026) reported on a 2024 report by Protecting Blue Whales and Blue Skies (BWBS). It gave “an 85 percent cooperation rate overall by fleets” and a 50 percent reduction in fatal strikes. The BWBS site states that participating vessels in the 2025 season “posed 40% less risk to whales when compared to the baseline of transits in the area in 2016”. On 21 May 2026 the same laboratory launched an AI thermal-camera system in San Francisco Bay. Nazario et al. (Cambridge Prisms: Coastal Futures, 24 June 2026) write that the initiative “has successfully helped improve voluntary vessel speed reduction cooperation”, citing whalesafe.com. The authors include Whale Safe's director Douglas McCauley and staff of its partner institutions, so their statement that the initiative helped improve cooperation comes from the system's makers. The cooperation and risk figures belong to the voluntary program of NOAA and BWBS. No cited source isolates Whale Safe's effect on any vessel. A separate record concerns a different system (the low-frequency detection and classification system, LFDCS, on gliders and a NOAA Right Whale Slow Zone). On 26 October 2026 the Whale Safe site listed the Santa Barbara acoustic system as offline.
purpose: Built to tell ship operators, in near real time, when whales are likely present in the shipping lanes. It also grades their cooperation with voluntary 10-knot zones so they slow down. The published ratings and report cards are that intended use.
system: Whale Safe (near real-time acoustic buoy with automated call detection and classification reviewed by analysts, naturalist sightings, WhaleWatch 2.0 blue whale habitat model, and AIS-based vessel speed report cards)
developer: Benioff Ocean Science Laboratory, Marine Science Institute, UC Santa Barbara, with Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, UC Santa Cruz, University of Washington, NOAA Southwest Fisheries Science Center and Conserve.io
deployer: Shipping companies transiting NOAA's voluntary vessel speed reduction zone in the Santa Barbara Channel; the Protecting Blue Whales and Blue Skies program
location: Santa Barbara Channel, California, United States

ratings.reason: Shipping lines' cooperation figures (59% of the time in 2023, per KCBX, and 85 percent fleet cooperation in a 2024 BWBS report) cover the whole voluntary program. No source attributes a change in any operator's behavior to Whale Safe's ratings or report cards.

The 50 percent reduction in fatal strikes in the 2024 report and the 40% lower risk in 2025 against a 2016 baseline are modeled estimates by BWBS for participating vessels. Neither figure counts whales saved, and no source attributes either to Whale Safe.

ai_role.statement: The automated detector on the buoy flags and classifies candidate whale calls, which an analyst confirms before they enter the daily rating. The habitat model is a statistical ensemble and the report cards are AIS arithmetic. The cooperation and risk figures belong to NOAA's and BWBS's voluntary slow-down program, which Whale Safe monitors and publicizes. No cited source separates Whale Safe's contribution from incentives, outreach and retailer pressure. The developer's own news office is the source of the claim that cooperation rose every year since launch.

Whale Safe's methodology page describes a moored acoustic buoy whose “tiny computer” detects and classifies blue, humpback and fin whale calls. Next, “An analyst then reviews these data and indicates for each 15-minute period whether each of the monitored species was detected”. The page also describes naturalist sightings through the Whale Alert and Spotter Pro apps, NOAA aerial surveys and the WhaleWatch 2.0 blue whale habitat model. These feed a daily Whale Presence Rating. Ship-tracking data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS) are used to grade each vessel's “cooperation rate” with the voluntary zone. UC Santa Barbara's news office (21 September 2022) called the buoy system “AI-powered”. It quoted director Douglas McCauley: “Every year since the original launch of Whale Safe we have seen an increase in ship cooperation rates”. KCBX (11 April 2024) reported from Whale Safe data: “in 2023, large vessels only slowed down 59% of the time in designated slow speed zones”. The Santa Barbara Independent (16 July 2026) reported on a 2024 report by Protecting Blue Whales and Blue Skies (BWBS). It gave “an 85 percent cooperation rate overall by fleets” and a 50 percent reduction in fatal strikes. The BWBS site states that participating vessels in the 2025 season “posed 40% less risk to whales when compared to the baseline of transits in the area in 2016”. On 21 May 2026 the same laboratory launched an AI thermal-camera system in San Francisco Bay. Nazario et al. (Cambridge Prisms: Coastal Futures, 24 June 2026) write that the initiative “has successfully helped improve voluntary vessel speed reduction cooperation”, citing whalesafe.com. The authors include Whale Safe's director Douglas McCauley and staff of its partner institutions, so their statement that the initiative helped improve cooperation comes from the system's makers. The cooperation and risk figures belong to the voluntary program of NOAA and BWBS. No cited source isolates Whale Safe's effect on any vessel. A separate record concerns a different system (the low-frequency detection and classification system, LFDCS, on gliders and a NOAA Right Whale Slow Zone). On 26 October 2026 the Whale Safe site listed the Santa Barbara acoustic system as offline.

ratings.reason: Shipping lines' cooperation figures (59% of the time in 2023, per KCBX, and 85 percent fleet cooperation in a 2024 BWBS report) cover the whole voluntary program. No source attributes a change in any operator's behavior to Whale Safe's ratings or report cards.

The 50 percent reduction in fatal strikes in the 2024 report and the 40% lower risk in 2025 against a 2016 baseline are modeled estimates by BWBS for participating vessels. Neither figure counts whales saved, and no source attributes either to Whale Safe.
